questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Choose packaging by physical protection, quantity and transport requirements.
questions.prompt: A cooperative must carry tomatoes over a rough road. It can use either a rigid ventilated crate or a sack that allows the fruit to be squeezed. Why is the crate the better choice?
options: Its sides help protect the fruit from crushing.
It seals out all air, which every fresh crop requires.
It makes sorting unnecessary even when some fruit is damaged.
It gives the same protection whether loosely filled or overloaded.
questions.answer: Its sides help protect the fruit from crushing.
questions.explanation: The rigid container supports and protects the produce during transport. Packaging does not guarantee price or remove other handling needs.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Choose packaging by physical protection, quantity and transport requirements.
questions.prompt: A seller has fitted egg trays and plain open baskets of the same capacity. Which feature makes the trays more suitable for loose eggs?
options: They allow heavy loads to rest directly on the shells.
They keep individual eggs apart and reduce collisions.
They are designed mainly to absorb liquid spilled from broken eggs.
They remove the need to secure the load during transport.
questions.answer: They keep individual eggs apart and reduce collisions.
questions.explanation: The shaped spaces support separate eggs, reducing movement and contact. The purpose is protection, not an increase in production.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Choose packaging by physical protection, quantity and transport requirements.
questions.prompt: Two buyers order the same dry produce: one wants small retail portions and the other wants a large wholesale load. Which packaging decision follows directly from the difference between their orders?
options: Use only large wholesale sacks for both orders to reduce packaging work.
Choose by package colour alone because the produce is identical.
Select package sizes suited to the quantity each buyer needs.
Use the largest available container even when most of it will be empty.
questions.answer: Select package sizes suited to the quantity each buyer needs.
questions.explanation: Order quantity and bulk influence package size. The same produce can require different sizes for retail and wholesale handling.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how production costs, quality and supply or demand can affect produce pricing.
questions.prompt: A farm’s irrigation and transport expenses rise while all other conditions are unchanged. Which consideration has most directly changed when the farmer reviews the selling price?
options: The quantity demanded by buyers.
The physical quality of the harvested crop.
The volume of produce offered in the market.
The cost of getting the produce ready for sale.
questions.answer: The cost of getting the produce ready for sale.
questions.explanation: Irrigation and transport are production or delivery costs relevant to pricing. The scenario does not establish that the farmer can pass every extra cost to buyers.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how production costs, quality and supply or demand can affect produce pricing.
questions.prompt: Several nearby farms harvest onions at the same time, increasing the amount offered for sale while buyers’ demand stays unchanged. What pressure would this normally place on the market price?
options: Downward pressure because supply has increased.
Upward pressure because the crop has become scarcer.
No pressure because supply cannot affect market price.
An automatic price increase matching the rise in harvest quantity.
questions.answer: Downward pressure because supply has increased.
questions.explanation: More supply with unchanged demand normally puts downward pressure on price. This is a direction of pressure, not a guaranteed numerical change.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how production costs, quality and supply or demand can affect produce pricing.
questions.prompt: At one stall, buyers pay more for properly sorted, undamaged mangoes than for bruised mangoes of the same total mass. Which price determinant is illustrated most clearly?
options: The total mass offered in each sale.
The quality of the produce offered.
A change in the distance to that stall.
A change in the number of sellers in the market.
questions.answer: The quality of the produce offered.
questions.explanation: The stated difference is condition and sorting quality. Equal mass alone does not require goods of different quality to sell for the same amount.

questions.learningObjective: Match farm information to suitable records and distinguish transaction evidence from summaries.
questions.prompt: A school farm wants to know how many watering cans and hoes it owns before buying more tools. Which existing record should it consult first?
options: A list of crops planned for next term.
A diary entry about yesterday’s rainfall.
An inventory listing the farm’s equipment.
A poster advertising vegetable sales.
questions.answer: An inventory listing the farm’s equipment.
questions.explanation: An inventory records the items held by the farm. A crop plan, weather diary or advertisement does not establish the current equipment stock.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Match farm information to suitable records and distinguish transaction evidence from summaries.
questions.prompt: The farm records the mass of vegetables harvested each day, including vegetables later eaten by the club rather than sold. What is the main purpose of this production record?
options: To prove that every harvested vegetable was sold.
To replace every purchase invoice.
To show only the cash collected from customers.
To track the quantity produced, regardless of its later use.
questions.answer: To track the quantity produced, regardless of its later use.
questions.explanation: A production record measures output. Sales and consumption are separate later uses and should not be confused with harvesting.

questions.prompt: A farm receives an invoice for seed bought on credit. Before entering the amount in a purchases record, what is the invoice primarily useful for?

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the elements used in constructing a woven textile.
questions.prompt: A learner twists short cotton fibres into a continuous strand before weaving. What is the resulting strand called?

Yarn.
Warp only.
Weft only.
questions.answer: Yarn.
questions.explanation: Yarn is a continuous strand made from fibres and used to make fabric. A hem and buttonhole are construction features made later.

questions.prompt: During a weaving demonstration, one set of threads is held lengthwise on the loom before the crossing threads are inserted. What is that lengthwise set called?

questions.explanation: The lengthwise threads are the warp. The weft passes across them during weaving.

questions.learningObjective: Classify textile fibres by origin without inferring all properties from appearance.
questions.prompt: A fabric label states that the fibre is cotton. Which origin places cotton in the natural-fibre group?
options: It comes from the cotton plant.
It is woven rather than knitted.
It can be dyed after manufacture.

questions.answer: It comes from the cotton plant.
questions.explanation: Cotton is a plant-derived fibre. Processing, dyeing and sewing do not change its classification by origin.

questions.subject: Pre-Vocational Studies
questions.learningObjective: Classify textile fibres by origin without inferring all properties from appearance.
questions.prompt: Two white shirts look similar, but one label says cotton and the other says polyester. What is the best reason to consult the labels before classifying their fibres?
options: White cloth must always be made from one fibre.
Similar prices prove that fibres have the same origin.
Appearance alone does not establish whether the fibre is natural or synthetic.
A sewn label turns any natural fibre into a synthetic one.
questions.answer: Appearance alone does not establish whether the fibre is natural or synthetic.
questions.explanation: Colour and appearance do not reliably identify fibre origin. The declared fibre composition gives information that looks alone cannot establish.

questions.learningObjective: Choose fabric-care actions using supplied composition and care instructions.
questions.prompt: A dark new scarf may release dye in water. Why would washing it separately at first help protect other clothes?
options: It reduces the chance of dye transferring to them.
It ensures the scarf will keep exactly the same colour.
It allows a higher wash temperature without checking the label.
It means the scarf no longer needs to be rinsed.
questions.answer: It reduces the chance of dye transferring to them.
questions.explanation: Keeping the scarf separate prevents released colour from contacting other garments during that wash. It does not establish permanent colourfastness.

questions.explanation: The bobbin holds the lower thread used to form the lockstitch with the needle thread. The other parts have different functions.

questions.learningObjective: Identify construction features by their purpose in shaping or finishing a garment.
questions.prompt: A dressmaker folds and stitches a tapered section of fabric so a garment fits the body more closely at the waist. Which feature is being made?

A dart.

questions.learningObjective: Identify construction features by their purpose in shaping or finishing a garment.
questions.prompt: The lower edge of a skirt is turned inward and stitched to finish it. What is this finished edge called?

A facing cut to the neckline shape.

questions.answer: A hem.
questions.explanation: A hem is formed by turning and securing an edge of the garment. It is an edge finish rather than a machine part or weaving thread.

questions.learningObjective: Identify construction features by their purpose in shaping or finishing a garment.
questions.prompt: A separate shaped piece is attached around a neckline and turned to the inside to finish the opening. What is that piece called?
options: A dart.
A hem made by turning the garment edge itself.
A tuck.
A facing.
questions.answer: A facing.
questions.explanation: A facing finishes and supports an edge such as a neckline or armhole from the inside. It is not the same as a dart used for shaping.
